LIBERAL CLUBS AT DARWEN AND ELSEWHERE. LORD Edward Cavendish and Mr. Cross the member tar Bolton, made capital speeches on Saturday at Over Damen, the occasion being the annual soiree of the three Liberal Clubs of that breezy and spirit stirring indus• trial community. Eight hundred people took tea together, and the cup that cheers on its own account seems to have inspired some of the heartiest cheering on the part of the partakers of it that has been heard in Damen since the oeuasion of the election in 1874, when Lord Edward Caven- dish and Sir Jame. K. Shuttleworth were the Liberal candidates for that divi- sion of the County of Lancaster, and so nearly achieved the swoons- they deserved, that thoir future return Os tolerably well assured. Liberal clubs are springing up on every side, and if any ngliala institution of reeent origin may be properly said to have a mission, that may be said of this the latest political organisation of the time. Nor do we deny that the same may be true of the Conservative clubs amongst us, wh eh may be said, perhaps, to be co-extensive with the Liberal institution. A somewhat important difference probably characterises them. We shall not be very wrong in affirming that whereas the Liberal club places polities first and social enjoyment after; its Conservative sour,- terpart certainly puts jollity first and lets politics lag a little in the . abject rear. In using the term polities however, it is neces- sary to discriminate. By politics we mean political discussion, political randy, political principle. The distinction between the two cleans of political club folk largely disap- pears if politico means, and means only, the spirit of ignorantly aealous, fiery, political partisanship. There is probably no zeal like blind coal; no force like the force of an uninformed and unbridled political fanaticism. The sudden aggre- gation of unintelligent social force found in the Conservative Clubs and Consti- tutional Associations of the tory party, es pecially in Lancashire, has aa yet, die- ' covered only one way of expreasing iteelf. It is— provisionally, at any rate, a huge re- freshment consuming performer on wind Instruments, and a rubicund—not to say ap- poplectio hastener to the Poll. It has not— and probably never will—for it is scarcely I "Pretty Fanny's way—arrived at the con- dition of being "sicklied o'er with the pale east of thought." The Liberal Club man, although he may have a decent appetite, and an unimpaired digestion, labours etill under an obvious disadvantage when compared with the political peony which blows and blazes in the Conservative parterre. For as we have often shown the Liberal of all ranks ia almost universally touched with the fine malady of thinking. Of him, it may be fairly mid that he is a thinker &at and a Liberal afterwards. We are, nevertheless, glad to remember that, although on the con- trary, the honest Conservative is a Conser- vative first and relegates thinking to quite a subordinate place, he does at intervals in- dulge in the rare luxury of refleotioe. For we by no means deny his capacity for inquiry or his susceptibility to the agencies of a political education. The Conservative Club will inevitably develope that capacity, and with character- istic slowness for which he is perhaps scarcely responsible—make those education,l agencies a reality of his existence. For even the members of • Conservative Club must sometimes talk Politics, and be now and then visited with file suspicion that after all, there may be something in that magical word which may mean more than sounding brass and tinkling cymbals or screaming "somebody for ever" at election times. In a word it is very likely that Conservative Clubs, when the first convivial ent•husiaem has got to be pretty well exhausted, will con- tract a taste for a more solid regimen. When that inevitable season comes, useful books will be consulted. History, Political Economy, Science, will lend their beneficent light to impart a meaning and vitality to politics, and the club, which at its beginning was a mere herd of gregarioue persons. bent almost exclusively on "bread and the circus," will enter on an education which will be of infinite use to the community, and afford new testimony that the Tory party out of Parliament, equally with the members of the party "educated "by the late Mr. Dis- raeli, most yield to the irresistible forms of the age, and advance to the political level

of it. The three Liberal Clubs of Darwen and their annual soiree have tempted us to make these passing observations on a new political institution, which seems likely to become no inconsiderable pow, r in England. and will have much to do in the future in moulding, and perhaps remodelling that public opinion which Parliament persistently consults, and to which the statesmen who are responsible for the peace and prosperity of the country constantly turn in our time to learn the as- pect of the political heavens.

div.head: DEFEAT OF THE CONFERENCE.
div.p: DEFEAT OF THE CONFERENCE.

The Great Powers of what we have been accustomed proudly to describe as civilised Europe, represented at Constantinople by their Plenipotentiaries, appear likely to be- come the victims of the most ignominious diplomatic failure known to the present cen- tury, or perhaps any other. During the present week the Conference has assembled day by day, and day by day its meeting has furnished the record of its own defeat. It is not, as we have for some time past shown, that the Conference owes ite failure to divided counsels, to unavowed diplomatic jealousies, to heterogeneous aims. The Envoys of the Powers have been wholly agreed as to the requirements to be sub- mitted to the Turkish Government; there has been no personal plotting for eupre- macy ; their objects have been alike and perfectly homogeneous. Lord Salisbury has shewn himself superior to the ignorant fears —or affectation of fears of Russia, which some of the leading journals of his party in England have of late unceasingly mani- fested. 'I he English Envoy has constantly acted at Constantinople in perfect accord with General Ignatieff, the Russian repre- sentative, and they in turn, as we have said. have done nothing to mar the unanimity of the Conference. Nor do the demands of the Powers seem to have suffered that daily abatement in political significance which the writers who ridicule the Conference delight to affirm. The Special Correspondent of the Daily News declares that the ultimatum is firmer in tone than was at first represented. The International Commission is still to be guided in its action by the instructions that were originally drawn upt and those inetruc- tions are strongly objected to by the Porte. There is but little modification of the pro- r male with regard to Montenegro and Servia. The rent of the original project of the Conference is retained nearly intact. There is meanwhile no indication that the Porte will yield on the question of the Inter- national Commission."

It is confidently stated that "the ultima- tum, as it is called, proposes a Commission of Control to see to the execution of reforms, and although it appears to have been stated in r ral diecuseion with the Turkish Plenipo- tentiariee that the Commission would not have executive power, no such restriction is contained in the written proposals of the Conference. Of course, to execute reforms and to see to the execution of reforms are different things. The Commission, without itself directiy and in the first instance pos- sessing executive power, may be endowed with authority to control the Executive, and 101111111 10 4011 01 10j9iteM

In the meantime the Grand Council of the Porte was to meet on Thursday to take into consideration the final proposals of the Powers, but it is not anticipated that the formal answer of She Sultan will be declared before Saturday.
